Surah al-Jinn

It is also called "Qul Uhiya ilayya" (Say: It has been revealed to me). It is Meccan by consensus, and its number of verses is twenty-eight without any dispute. As for its connection (wajh al-ittisal) with the preceding surah, al-Jalal al-Suyuti said: "I reflected on it for a period, and nothing became clear to me except that He, glory be to Him, said in Surah Nuh (10-11): ﴿Ask your Lord for forgiveness; indeed He is ever Forgiving﴾ ﴿He will send down upon you abundant rain from the sky﴾. And He, mighty and majestic, said in this surah to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿And if they had remained on the path, We would have given them abundant water to drink﴾ [al-Jinn: 16]. This is a clear connection." End of quote. Regarding his words "to the disbelievers of Makkah" there is something you will learn, God willing. It may also be added that this surah includes mention of something related to the sky, as the previous surah does, and the mention of punishment for one who disobeys Allah, mighty and majestic, in His words: ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger, then indeed for him is the fire of Hell, abiding therein forever﴾ [al-Jinn: 23], which in a certain respect corresponds to His words: ﴿They were drowned and then made to enter a fire﴾ [Nuh: 25].

Abu Hayyan said on this matter: when He, exalted, related the persistence of the people of Nuh in disbelief and their devotion to the worship of idols, and he was the first Messenger to the people of the earth, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) is the last Messenger to the people of the earth, and the Arabs, of whom he (ﷺ) is one, were worshippers of idols like the people of Nuh, to the extent that they worshipped idols similar to those idols in names, or even identical to them, and what he (peace and blessings be upon him) brought was guiding to right guidance, and the Arabs heard it, but most of them hesitated to believe in him, Allah revealed Surah al-Jinn and placed it right after Surah Nuh as a rebuke to the Quraysh and the Arabs for their slowness in believing, while the jinn were better than them, since those among them who accepted faith did so, and they are not of the same kind as the Messenger (peace be upon him), to the point that they nearly became a crowd around him (libad). Yet despite this slowness, they (the Arabs) denied him and what he brought, out of envy and rebellion against Allah sending down His bounty upon whomever He wills of His servants. So the Mighty One, who has no equal, said: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾. Ibn Abi 'Abla, al-Ataki from Abu 'Amr, and Ju'ba ibn 'A'idh al-Asadi read "Wuhhiya" without a hamza, and it has the meaning of "Uhiya" with the hamza. From it is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

"Wuhhiya laha al-qararu
fastaqarrat"

Zayd ibn 'Ali, and Ju'ba, as transmitted from him by al-Kisa'i, and Ibn Abi 'Abla in one narration, read "Uhhiya," substituting a hamza for the waw of "wuhhiya," as they say "u'idda" for "wu'ida." Al-Zamakhshari said: this is from absolute metathesis (al-qalb al-mutlaq), its permissibility in every damma-d waw. Al-Mazini also allowed it in the kasra-d case, such as "ishah" and "i'a'" and "isadah." This is one of the two opinions of al-Mazini; the other opinion restricts it to what is heard. What he mentioned about the absolute permissibility in the damma-d case has been criticized on the grounds that the damma may occur initially, medially, and finally, each with its own rules, and some of these are disputed and detailed in the books of grammar, so let it be consulted. Some of the eminent scholars added the conversion of the waw and of the letter preceding the damma, saying that this too is regular and systematic, and that it occurs in the fatha-d case as well, as in "a'ad" (for "ahad"). In all readings the preposition phrase (al-jarr) is connected to what precedes it, and the deputy subject (naib al-fa'il) is ﴿annahu﴾ etc., with "annahu" being in the position of a verbal noun (masdar), and the pronoun referring to the matter/case (li-l-sha'n). ﴿Istama'a﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, as mentioned in al-Ahqaf, and its object has been omitted due to the indication of what follows it. ﴿A group (nafar) of the jinn﴾. The nafar, according to the well-known usage, is from three to ten.

Al-Hariri said in his Durrah: the nafar applies only to three men up to ten, and he was mistaken in this, for it may be used for more than ten in eloquent usage, and many people of lexicography mentioned it. In the speech of al-Sha'bi: "Dathana bidh'at 'ashara nafaran" (a number of men told me). It is not restricted to men, nor even to people, since it is applied here to the jinn. In al-Mujmal: the rahT and the nafar are used up to forty. The difference between them is that the rahT (the rahT) go back to one father, unlike the nafar, and it may be applied to a people. From it is His saying, exalted: ﴿And mightier in numbers (a'azz nafaran)﴾ [al-Kahf: 34], and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"fahuwa la tanmi ramiyyatuhu * ma lahu la 'udda min nafarih"

Al-Imam al-Kirmani said that the nafar has another meaning in common usage, which is "a man," and by "common usage" he meant the usage of the language, since the authentic hadith was explained with it, so let this be remembered. ﴿And the jinn﴾: its singular is jinni, like Rum and Rumi. They are rational bodies in which the fiery nature predominates, as His saying, exalted, testifies: ﴿And He created the jinn from a smokeless flame of fire﴾ [al-Rahman: 15]. It has been said that they are airy, all of them or a kind of them, capable of taking various forms; their nature is concealment, and they may be seen in forms other than their original forms, and even in their original forms in which they were created, as with the angels, peace be upon them. This applies to the prophets, the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, and whomever Allah, mighty and majestic, wills among His special servants. They have strength for arduous tasks, and there is no rational obstacle to some of the subtle fiery bodies differing from the other kinds of subtle bodies in their essence, and they are receptive to the bestowal of life and the capacity for wondrous acts, for example.

The people of the New Philosophy have spoken of subtle bodies to which they attributed properties that dazzle the minds, so the bodies of the jinn may be of that kind. The realm of nature is too vast for the understanding to encompass what has been deposited in it. Most philosophers deny the jinn.

In Ibn Sina's Risalat al-Hudud: "The jinni is an airy animal that takes on various forms." This explains the name, and its apparent meaning is a denial that this reality has existence outside the mind, and denying that is manifest disbelief, as is not hidden. A great many of the early philosophers and the people of spiritual sciences acknowledged their existence, and they call them the lower spirits (al-arwah al-sufliyyah). What is well known is that they claimed they are substances subsisting by themselves, not bodies nor corporeal, and that they are different kinds in essence, like the differing essences of accidents; some of them are good and some evil, and none knows the number of their kinds and categories except Allah, mighty and majestic. It is not far-fetched on this view that among their kinds there are some that can perform arduous, great acts that humans cannot. Indeed, it is not far-fetched, as has been said, that each kind of them has a connection with a particular kind of bodies of this world. Some people claimed that human spirits and rational souls, when they separate from their bodies, increase in strength and perfection because of what is disclosed to them of spiritual secrets in that spiritual world; so when a body similar to the body that belonged to that separated soul happens to come into existence, that soul attaches to it in some way and becomes like an assistant to the soul of that body in its actions and management of that body. If this occurs with good souls, that helper is called an angel (malak), and that assistance is called inspiration (ilham); if it occurs with evil souls, that helper is called a devil (shaytan), and that assistance is called whispering (waswasah). All of this contradicts the sayings of the early generations (al-salaf).

The apparent meaning of the verses and hadiths, and the majority of the followers of religions, acknowledge their existence, as do the Muslims, even though they differ regarding their reality. The complete discussion of this matter is sought from "Akam al-Marjan." In al-Tafsir al-Kabir there is a portion related to this; return to it if you wish.

They differed regarding the number of those who listened. It was said they were seven: according to Zirr, three from the people of Harran and four from the people of Nasibayn, a village in Yemen other than the village in Iraq. According to Ikrimah, they were twelve thousand from the island of Mosul. And whether they were seven or nine out of twelve thousand, perhaps the nafar refers to the group. In al-Kashshaf: they were from the Shaysaban, who are the most numerous of the jinn, and most of Iblis's soldiers are from them. The verse clearly shows that he (ﷺ) knew of their listening through revelation, not through direct observation, and it occurs in the hadiths that he (peace be upon him) saw them; the reconciliation of this is by the multiplicity of the incident.

In Akam al-Marjan he said, summarized: in the two Sahihs, in the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not recite to the jinn, nor see them. He only set out with a group of the Companions toward the market of 'Ukaz, when the jinn had been prevented from the sky by meteors. They said: 'This is only because something has happened; strike the eastern and western parts of the earth.' So those who went toward Tihamah among them passed by him (peace be upon him) while he was praying the dawn prayer with his Companions at Nakhlah. When they heard him, they said: 'This is what has come between us and the sky,' and they returned to their people and said: 'O our people, etc.' Then Allah revealed to him: ﴿Say: It has been revealed to me﴾, etc." Then he said: Ibn 'Abbas's denial refers only to this incident, and their hearing of his recitation (ﷺ) at dawn in this incident, not absolutely. This is indicated by His saying, exalted: ﴿And when We turned toward you a group of the jinn﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 29], etc., for it indicates that he (peace be upon him) spoke to them, called them, and made them messengers to those other than them, as al-Bayhaqi said. Abu Dawud related from 'Alqamah, from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went with him and recited the Qur'an to them." He said: "He took us along and showed us their traces and the traces of their fires," etc. The hadiths indicate that the jinn's delegations occurred six times.

Ibn Taymiyyah said: Ibn 'Abbas knew what the Qur'an indicates, but did not know what Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurayrah knew of the jinn coming to him (ﷺ) and speaking with him (peace be upon him). The story of the jinn occurred three years before the Hijrah. Al-Waqidi said it was in the eleventh year of prophethood, and Ibn 'Abbas had nearly reached puberty at the Farewell Pilgrimage. So you know that the story of the jinn occurred six times.

In the Sharh of al-Bayhaqi, from various routes, from Ibn Mas'ud: "The Prophet (ﷺ) prayed the 'Isha prayer, then departed, took my hand until we reached a certain place, had me sit, drew a line around me, and said: 'Do not leave your line.' While I was sitting, men of them came to me, as if they were Zutt, and he related a long hadith; and that he (ﷺ) did not come until the dawn. He said: I began to hear voices. Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) came, and I said: 'Where were you, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'The jinn sent for me.' I said: 'What are these voices that were heard?' He said: 'They are their voices when they bade me farewell and greeted me.'"

The disagreement regarding few and many may be reconciled by saying that this is also due to the multiplicity of the incident. And Allah knows best. It was differed regarding what they heard: 'Ikrimah said: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1]. It was also said: Surah al-Rahman. ﴿Then they said﴾, i.e., to their people upon their return to them: ﴿Indeed we have heard a Qur'an﴾, i.e., a book being recited, as one of the eminent scholars explained it, and it was explained this way to indicate that what they mentioned of its description that follows is a description of the whole of it, not merely of what was recited from it. The meaning is that it is from the heavenly scriptures, and the tanwin is for magnification, i.e., a Qur'an of exalted status. ﴿Wondrous (ajaban)﴾: unique, distinct from human speech in beauty of arrangement and subtlety of meaning. It is a verbal noun (masdar) described by it for emphasis.

﴿يَهْدِي إلى الرُّشْدِ﴾ ("He guides to the right course") means: to the truth and to what is correct. It was also said: to tawhid (the oneness of God) and to faith. ʿIsa (Ibn ʿUmar) read «الرُّشُدِ» with two dammas, and it is also reported from him that he read both with fatha. ﴿فَآمَنّا بِهِ﴾ ("so we believed in it") means: in that Qur'an, without delay. ﴿ولَنْ نُشْرِكَ بِرَبِّنا أحَدًا﴾ ("and we will never associate anyone with our Lord") means: in accordance with what its proofs of tawhid express, or in accordance with what the rational proofs for tawhid express. This clause is not joined with the particle fa' (so).

[Page 84]

Al-Khafaji said: this is because their denial of association (shirk) is either based on the rational proof that was established for them, in which case its consequence does not follow from belief in the Qur'an; or it is based on what they heard from the Qur'an, in which case it suffices for its consequence to follow from it that the first clause is joined by fa'. Especially since the bāʾ in «بِهِ» may indicate causation, so that belief in it includes belief in what is in it. For when you say, "I struck him, so he behaved properly and submitted to me," the submission is understood as a consequence of the striking. But if you said, "so he submitted," it would not be a consequence of the first clause, but of what preceded it.

It was also said: the clause is joined with waw, and this leaves the determination of the sequence to the mind of the listener. It may be said that the whole of ﴿فَآمَنّا بِهِ ولَنْ نُشْرِكَ﴾ is caused by the whole of ﴿إنّا سَمِعْنا﴾ and so on. Thus its being a miraculous Qur'an necessitates belief in it, and its guiding to right conduct necessitates uprooting shirk from its base. The first is better. It is also permitted that the pronoun in «بِهِ» refers to God, the Mighty and Majestic, because His saying ﴿بِرَبِّنا﴾ ("our Lord") explains it. So do not be heedless.

﴿And that He, exalted is He, is the majesty of our Lord﴾. The readers differed over the recitation of this and what follows it, up to ﴿and that among us are the Muslims﴾. There are twelve such instances. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf and Hafs read them all with a *fath* (the vowel *a*) on the *hamzah* (أنَّ). Abu Ja'far agreed with them on the three occurrences here, and in ﴿and that he used to say﴾ and ﴿and that there were men﴾. The rest read them all with a *kasr* (the vowel *i*) on the *hamzah* (إنَّ). They agreed on the *fath* in ﴿that he (the one) listened﴾ and ﴿and that the mosques﴾ [al-Hajj: 18], because these cannot be part of the words of the jinn but are rather what was revealed. The rest, however, can be part of their words and also of what was revealed.

They differed over the reading of ﴿that when he stood up﴾: Nafi' and Abu Bakr read it with a *kasr*, and the rest with a *fath*. This is how some of the eminent scholars distinguished it, and it is the reliable position. The justification for the *kasr* in ﴿that this and what follows it, up to ﴿and that among us are the Muslims﴾ is clear, like the *kasr* in ﴿Indeed, we have heard a wondrous Qur'an﴾, since the clauses are plainly coordinated with the reported speech following "said" and clearly fall under it.

As for the justification for the *fath*, it is obscure, and for this reason it has been disputed. al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari said that it is coordination with the position (*mahall*) of the prepositional phrase in ﴿so we believed in Him﴾, as if it were said: "We believed in it, and we believed that He, exalted is He, is the majesty of our Lord, and that our foolish one used to say..." and so on for the rest. Showing the position is achieved by repeating the preposition with its synonym. Coordinating with a pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition is not permitted according to the Basrans, though it is according to the Kufans, who permit it; and if it is said that here it is by way of an implied preposition, because its deletion before *anna* and *inna* is regular, that would be sound, as in al-Kashf. Makki weakened coordination with what is in the scope of "we believed", saying: "There is a semantic remoteness, because they did not report that they believed on the ground that when they heard the guidance they believed in it, nor that they believed that there were men. Rather, God the Exalted related about them that they said this, reporting about themselves to their companions." It has been answered on behalf of those who adopt this view that belief and affirmation are appropriate in some of those coordinated items without doubt, and so it extends to the rest and is understood in terms of meaning, in the manner of his saying: (*And they arched the eyebrows and the eyes*). It is thus interpreted in the same way as similar cases: our "believing" is construed as encompassing all of them, or with each one a fitting verb is supplied.

Abu Hatim said that it is coordination with the deputy subject (*na'ib al-fa'il*) of "it was revealed", namely "that he listened", as in ﴿that the mosques﴾, on the basis that what was revealed is the very wording of the jinn, by way of reported speech, as if it were said: ﴿Say: it was revealed to me﴾ such-and-such, and such-and-such, and these expressions. This was criticized on the ground that reporting their expressions requires that *anna* in their speech be with a *fath* on the *hamzah*, and this would not be evident unless their speech contained something that requires the *fath*, such as "listen", "know", or "we inform you", but they omitted the time of the reporting, and no reason for its omission is apparent. Even if it were apparent, the *fath* would not be due to coordination, since the deputy subject refers to the whole of each clause, taking the wording into account, not the compound of *anna* and what follows it; otherwise it would not be correct to say "what was revealed is such-and-such and such-and-such."

As for these expressions: if *anna* in their speech was with a *kasr* on the *hamzah*, and the claim that reported speech requires the *fath* is valid while these expressions are still intended with it, then that is the case. Otherwise the matter is as you see. Understand this and consider it carefully.

*al-jadd* means greatness and majesty. It is said: *jadda fi 'aynī*, i.e. it became great in my eyes, and *jalla*, i.e. it was exalted. The meaning is: "And we affirm that the affair has risen in greatness and majesty, our Lord's greatness having become great, may He be mighty and exalted." There is in this a great deal of emphasis that is not hidden.

Abu 'Ubaydah and al-Akhfash said that *al-jadd* means dominion and sovereignty. It was also said that it means wealth, and this is reported from Anas and al-Hasan regarding the verse. The first is reported from the majority. *Al-jadd* in all these senses is used metaphorically from *al-jadd*, which means fortune (*al-bakht*). His saying, may He be mighty and exalted, ﴿He has not taken a consort nor a son﴾ is an explanation of the clause and a statement of its ruling, and for this reason it is not coordinated with it. So the meaning is to describe Him, mighty and exalted, as transcendent above having a consort or a son, owing to His greatness, or His sovereignty, or His wealth, glory be to Him and exalted. It seems that they heard from the Qur'an what alerted them to the error of the belief held by the unbelieving jinn, who likened Him, glory be to Him, to His creation in taking a consort and a son, so they magnified Him and declared Him exalted above that.

Hamid ibn Qays read *jud* with a *damma* on the *jim*. Abu Hayyan said in al-Bahr that its meaning is "the Great", reported by Sibawayh. Its annexation to ﴿our Lord﴾ is an annexation of the attribute to the qualified noun, and the meaning is: "Exalted is our Lord, the Great."

'Ikrimah read *jaddun* with tanwin and a *damma*, and ﴿Lord﴾ in the nominative. It was analyzed as *jadd* meaning "the Great" also, and *rabbuna* is the predicate of an omitted subject, i.e. "He is our Lord," or an apposition to *jaddun*.

He also read *jadan* with tanwin and a *fatha*, as a specifying accusative (*tamyīz*) transferred from the subject. He, and Qatadah, also read *jidan* with a *kasr* on the *jim*, tanwin and a *fatha*, and ﴿Lord﴾ in the nominative. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: *jidan* is in the accusative as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*), and the meaning is: "Exalted is our Lord in truth and in full power." Others said it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, i.e. "an exalting, a great one."

Ibn al-Sumaifa' read *jida rabbina*, meaning: His bounty and benefit, glory be to Him. The intended meaning here is wealth, so do not be heedless.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 4:

﴿And that it was that our foolish one (safihuna) used to say﴾ — according to the majority (al-jumhur), this is Iblis; and it was said that it refers to the rebellious ones (maradat) among the jinn. The idafa (genitive construction) is to the genus, and what is meant is "our foolish ones" (safihauna). ﴿an outrageous transgression against God﴾ — that is, a statement containing shatat (shatat: extreme deviation), meaning a distance from moderation and a crossing of bounds; or it is itself a shatat, due to the extreme remoteness of its speaker from the truth, namely the attribution of a consort and a son to Him, exalted and majestic is He. The connection of faith and belief (al-iman wa-al-tasdiq) to this statement, based on what the conjunction (al-atf) requires with respect to what falls within the scope of ﴿fa-amanna (so we believed)﴾, is not in regard to the statement itself, for they had known beforehand what their foolish one had said; rather it is in regard to its being a shatat. It is as if it were said: "and we affirmed that what our foolish one used to say concerning Him, glorified is He, was a shatat."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 5:

﴿And we thought that no human or jinn would ever speak a lie against Allah.﴾ This is an excuse from them for their blind following (taqlid) of their foolish one. That is, "We used to think that no one would lie against Allah the Exalted, so that they would attribute to Him, glorified is He, a consort and a son. For this reason we believed the foolish one's statement to be true." Perhaps faith (al-iman) is linked to what their speech implies and what follows from their error in their assumption, as if it were said: "And we confirmed, through our error in the assumption on account of which we believed what we believed." The word *kadhiban* (a lie) is a verbal noun (masdar) functioning as an emphasizing object (mu'akkid) of *taqul* (speak), because it is a type of speech, as in *qa'adtu al-qurfusa'* ("I sat in the crouching posture"). Or it is a qualifier of a deleted verbal noun, meaning "a speech that is a lie," i.e., "a speech in which lying is found," because the emission of lying from Him (the Exalted) is inconceivable, even though He is famously described with it, like the one who says [something false]. It is also permitted that it is a description by means of a verbal noun for the sake of emphasis (mubalaghah), and this relates to the negation and not to what is negated.

The reciters al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakrah, Ya'qub and Ibn Miqsam read *taqulu* (with a dammah on the lam, as an imperfect verb) "*taqulu*," whose original form is *tatafawwalu* with two *ta'*s, one of which was deleted. Then *kadhiban* is a verbal noun serving as an emphasizing object, because lying is speaking (*al-taqawwul*).

﴿And that there were men among mankind who sought refuge with men among the jinn﴾. A man among the Arabs, when night fell on him in a barren valley and he feared for himself, would call out at the top of his voice: "O Mighty One of this valley, I seek refuge with You from the fools who are in Your obedience," meaning the jinn and their chief. When they heard that, they became arrogant and said, "We have become masters of the jinn and of mankind." This is the meaning of His words, ﴿so they increased them﴾, i.e., the men who sought refuge increased the jinn ﴿in rahaqan﴾, i.e., in arrogance and insolence. So the pronoun in the nominative refers to the men of mankind, since they are the ones being spoken of, and the pronoun in the accusative refers to the men of the jinn. This is the view of Mujahid, al-Nakha'i, Ubayd ibn Umayr, and a group of others. However, some of them interpreted rahaq as sin, and al-Tabari cited for this the verse of al-A'sha:

"Nothing benefits me except seeing her; the lover does not complain as long as he has not fallen into rahaq."

He meant: as long as he has not touched what is forbidden. So the meaning here is that they increased mankind and the jinn in sin, because they (the men) exalted them (the jinn), so the jinn increased them in making lawful the prohibitions of Allah, the Exalted. Or, the jinn increased the men who sought refuge in ghayy (error), by misleading them until they sought refuge with them. In this case the two pronouns are reversed from what came before. This is the view of Qatadah, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Rabi', and Ibn Zayd. The fa' (ف, "so") according to the first interpretation indicates sequence (al-ta'qib, "immediate consequence"), and according to this view it has been said that it indicates the sequence of reporting (al-tartib al-ikhbari, "sequence in narration").

Al-Farra' held that what follows the fa' may come before it when indicated by evidence, as in His words, ﴿How many a town We destroyed, and Our punishment came upon it﴾ [al-A'raf: 4]. The majority of grammarians disagree with him. It has also been said that there is an omission in the sentence, meaning: "So they followed them, and they increased them."

The verse clearly indicates that the word rijal (men) is applied to male jinn just as it is applied to male humans. It has also been said that it is not applied to male jinn.

The phrase ﴿among the jinn﴾ in the verse is connected to ﴿seek refuge﴾, and its meaning is that there were men of mankind who sought refuge from the evil of the jinn with men of mankind. A man would say, for example, "I seek refuge with Hudhayfah ibn Badr from the jinn of this valley." This is a strange view, contrary to what the majority holds, supported by reports. Perhaps the connection of the faith to this (interpretation) is in view of what it implies, namely that this is misguidance which necessarily increases rahaq.

Some reports have come containing what is to be said instead of this seeking of refuge. In a long hadith that Abu Nasr al-Sajzi recorded in al-Ibanah through the chain of Mujahid from Ibn Abbas, and said: "very strange indeed," that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If any of you is seized by fear, or alights in a land of jinn, let him say: 'I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah, which no pious nor wicked person can transgress, from the evil of what enters the earth and what comes out of it, what descends from the sky and what ascends into it, and from the trials of the day and the visitors of the night, except a visitor who comes with good.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 7:

﴿And that they thought﴾, i.e., the humans, ﴿as you thought﴾, O jinn, ﴿that Allah would never raise up anyone﴾, i.e., of the messengers, to any of the servants. It is also said that He, glory be to Him, would never raise up anyone after death. Whichever is meant, the implication is: ﴿they erred and you erred.﴾ Perhaps this relates to the (technical term: al-iman, the object of belief) ... It is also said that the meaning is: the jinn thought, as you thought, O disbelievers, that ﴿never...﴾ etc., so this verse is part of the speech that was revealed, coordinated with His words, exalted is He, ﴿that he listened﴾.

And upon the reading with the kasra (i.e., ﴿innahu﴾), it is a resumption of His speech, exalted is He, and likewise what precedes it, according to what has been said. In al-Kashshaf it is said: it has been said that the two verses, meaning this one and His words, exalted is He, ﴿and that there were men﴾ etc., are part of what was revealed. This was criticised in al-Kashf on the grounds that there is weakness in it, because His words, glory be to Him...

﴿And that we touched the sky﴾ and what follows is part of the speech of the jinn, or of what they affirmed (saddaqahu) according to the two readings, because it is part of what was revealed to him. So the intervening material is not an impermissible parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ), unless it is interpreted as functioning in that manner, in that it confirms what came from them earlier concerning their persistence in disbelief. The strain in this is not hidden. End of quotation.

Abu al-Su'ud chose, in all the sentences introduced by "annā," that they are coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿that he listened﴾, in the manner you heard from Abu Hatim, and you have already heard what is in it. "Anna" is the light (mukhaffafah) form of the heavy "anna," its noun being the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n), and the clause after it is its predicate. The clause "that he will never raise up" and so on, it was said, fills the place of the two objects of "ẓannū" (they thought). He also allowed that it fills the place of the two objects of "ẓanantum" (you thought), with the first object omitted, as is preferred in such cases.

He preferred the first option in the verse on the ground that ﴿ẓannū﴾ is the intended verb there, so making the mentioned object its complement is better. As for ﴿as you thought﴾, it is mentioned incidentally. From this it is known that the preference for applying the second verb in the case of tanāzuʿ (the dispute over a shared governing word) is not absolute.

﴿And that we touched the sky﴾: that is, we sought to reach it in order to hear the speech of its inhabitants, or we sought its news. It was said that "lams" (touching) is used figuratively from "massa" (touching) for "seeking," as in "jass" (feeling). One says: lamasahu, iltamasahu, and talammasahu, like ṭalabahu, aṭlabahu, and taṭallabahu.

The apparent view is that the figure of speech here is lexical (lughawiyyah), because it is a majāz mursal (metonymy) in using the word for a necessary consequence of its meaning. "Listening" is taken in its literal sense.

﴿But we found it﴾: that is, we encountered it and reached it. So "wajada" is transitive to one object. His saying, exalted is He, ﴿filled﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with or without "qad" being presumed. Even if "wajada" is one of the verbs of the heart (af'āl al-qulūb), this clause is then in the position of the second object. Al-A'raj read "mulyat" with a ya' without a hamza.

﴿guards﴾: that is, ḥaras is an ism jam' (collective noun), like khadam, as one group has held, because it follows a pattern that is common among singular nouns, such as baṣar and qamar. For this reason it is attributed to it, so one says ḥarasī. Some have held that it is a plural, but the correct view is the first. For this reason it is described with the singular, so it says ﴿severe﴾, that is, strong. Similar to this is the line of verse:

I built it with a band of my own wealth, fearing a little infantry and a cavalry of raiders.

If its meaning were treated as plural, one would say shidād (severe, plural), except that one looks to the apparent form of the pattern faʿīl, for it applies equally to the singular and the plural. The intended meaning of ḥaras is the angels, peace be upon them, who prevent them from approaching the sky.

﴿and meteors﴾: the plural of shihāb, and the discussion of it has already passed. Some have allowed that ḥaras means the meteors, and the conjunction is then like his saying:

And Hind came from beyond it, distance and remoteness.

This is contrary to the apparent meaning. The inclusion of "annā lamasnā" and so on within the scope of belief (īmān), and likewise most of the clauses that follow, is extremely obscure. The apparent view is to assume something like "we shall inform you" regarding what its inclusion within that is not evident, or to interpret "āmannā min awwal al-amr" (we believed from the very beginning) in a way that applies to all of them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 9:

﴿And that we used to sit﴾ before this ﴿in it﴾, i.e., in the heaven, ﴿in positions for hearing﴾, i.e., positions existing for hearing, free of guards and meteors; or suitable for watching and listening. (﴿for hearing﴾) is connected to "we used to sit", i.e., for the sake of hearing; or it is connected to an implied verb, and it is an attribute of "positions". The manner of their sitting, as it is said, is that some of them ride upon others. A raised (marfu') report has been related concerning this. It is also said there is no obstacle to it being by the ascent of whichever of them wills, by himself, to the place from which he can hear the speech.

﴿So whoever listens now﴾. In the explanation of al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil) it is said: "(now) here means nearness, metaphorically, so it is valid with the past and the future." In al-Bahr it is said that it is a time adverb for the present. "(listens)" is in the future, but the adverb was extended and used for the future, as the poet said:

"I will strive now, when its time has come"

So the meaning is: whoever happens to listen in the coming time ﴿will find for himself a watching meteor﴾, i.e., he will find a meteor watching over him, and for its sake it turns him away from listening by stoning. So "watching" (rasadan) is an attribute of "meteor" (shihaban). If it is singular, the matter is clear; if it is a collective noun for "watcher," like "guards" (haras), then describing the singular by it is because the meteor, due to the intensity of its prevention and burning, is treated as if it were meteors. An analogy for this is the description of "ma'a" (singular of intestines) as "hungry" (jiya') in the verse of al-Qatami:

"As if the shackles of my legs, when they gathered, were the pulling ropes of a saddle or hungry intestines"

He also permitted that it be an object of purpose, i.e., for the sake of watching. It has been said it may be a collective noun functioning as an attribute of what precedes it, by estimating "possessors of a meteor," so it is as if it were said: he will find for himself possessors of meteors watching for stoning, and they are the angels, peace be upon them, who stone them with meteors and prevent them from listening. But this is far-fetched.

In the verse there is a refutation of those who claim that the stoning occurred after the mission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, which is one of his signs, peace and blessings be upon him, since it is said in it "they were filled." It is, as al-Jahiz said, clear that the newly occurring matter is the filling and the increase. Likewise is the statement of Allah, glorified is He, ﴿we used to sit in it in positions﴾, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, so it is as if it were said: we used to find in it some positions free from guards and meteors, but now all the positions are filled ﴿so whoever listens﴾, etc. The presence of meteors before their mention is also shown in pre-Islamic poetry. Bishr ibn Abi Khazim said:

"The caravan, dust overtakes it and its foal, it swoops behind them like the swooping of a star"

Aws ibn Hajar said:

"It swooped like a shooting star, followed by dust rising, you would think it a tent-rope"

Awf ibn al-Kharia said, describing a horse:

"It turns back to us the caravan away from its herd, or the bull, like a shooting star pursued by blood"

As al-Tabrizi said, all these poets are pre-Islamic (jahiliyya); among them there is no mukhadram.

And what al-Zuhri related from Ali ibn al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, from Ibn Abbas: "While the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was sitting with a group of the Ansar, a star shot and lit up, so he said: 'What did you used to say about the like of this in the Jahiliyya?' They said: 'We used to say a great one dies or a great one is born.'"

It is related from Ma'mar: I said to al-Zuhri: "Was there shooting of stars in the Jahiliyya?" He said: "Yes." I said: "What do you think of His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and that we used to sit﴾?" He said: "It became severe and its matter was intensified when the Prophet ﷺ was sent," and it seems he took that also from the verse.

Some said: the shooting did not exist at first; then it occurred to prevent [the jinn] from some of the heavens; then it increased and the devils were prevented from all of them on the day the Prophet, peace be upon him, was made a prophet. It was also permitted that the meteors existed before for natural events, not at all for preventing the devils. The occurrence after the mission is the shooting of the devils with them, in the sense that when they ascend for listening they are shot at; so it does not also necessarily follow that everything that occurs today of meteors is for shooting, but it may be for other matters, by causes known to Allah, exalted is He. This is answered regarding the occurrence of meteors in the month of Ramadan, along with what has come that the rebellious devils are chained in it. For those who say meteors only occur for shooting there is another answer, mentioned in its place.

They mentioned their finding the positions filled with guards and the complete prevention of eavesdropping. It was said: this is an explanation of what drove them to travel in the lands until they came upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and heard his recitation, peace and blessings be upon him, and their saying.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 10:

﴿And that we do not know whether evil is intended for those who are on the earth﴾ by the guarding of the heaven ﴿or whether their Lord intends for them guidance (rashad)﴾, i.e., good, as a continuation of that. The real impetus was the change of the state from what they had been accustomed to, and the sense that it was for a grave matter, and the eagerness to be informed of it fully. And it is not hidden what courtesy there is in their saying ﴿evil is intended﴾ and so on, in that they did not explicitly attribute evil to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as they did explicitly with good, even though the doer of everything is Allah, exalted is He. Indeed, they combined courtesy and good belief.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 11:

﴿And among us are the righteous﴾: that is, those described by good condition in their own affairs and in their dealings with others, inclining toward good and righteousness as sound natural disposition requires, not toward evil and corruption as wicked souls incline. ﴿And among us are others below that﴾: that is, people below that described level. The omission of the described noun is common when it is part of a noun governed by min (من) placed before it, and the description is an adverbial phrase, as here, or a clause, as in His saying: "Min-na aqama wa-min-na za'ana" (some of us stayed and some of us traveled). By "these people" they mean those who are moderate in good condition in the aforementioned manner, not in faith and piety, as some have said, for this is a description of their state before hearing the Qur'an, as indicated by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿We were divided into diverse ways﴾.

As for their state after hearing it, it will be related by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And when we heard the guidance﴾ up to His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And among us are the Muslims﴾, etc. Some have permitted that ﴿dun﴾ (دُونَ) means "other than" (غَيْرَ), so that ﴿dun dhalika﴾ would include the purely wicked. In either case, the clause ﴿kunna...﴾ etc. is an explanation of the preceding division. However, it has been said that the more suitable reading on this is that dun means "other than," and the speech is elliptical of a noun: i.e., "we were people of ways," that is, doctrines; or "like ways" in differing conditions; or "our ways were diverse ways" (qidad). That this is from the figure of speech of meeting caravans (talaqqi al-rukban) is not to be considered, and not regarding it as an eloquent simile so as to dispense with estimating something like qil (قيل), because the context is not one of hyperbole.

Al-Zamakhshari permitted that ﴿ta'ā'iq﴾ (طَرائِقَ) be in the accusative as an adverb of place, with an implied fi (في), i.e., "we were in ﴿ta'ā'iq﴾." This was criticized on the grounds that tariq (طريق) is a specific noun for a place one traverses, so one does not say of a house or a mosque that it is a tariq in an absolute sense; rather one says "I made the mosque a tariq," and thus such a noun is not put in the adverbial accusative except in cases of necessity. Sibawayh explicitly stated that his saying, "kama 'asala al-tariqa al-tha'lab" (as the fox swirled the path), is anomalous, so the noble Qur'an is not to be construed according to that. Some grammarians said: it is a general adverb, because every place is traversed by a path, and qidad means scattered, differing ones. The poet said:

"The Restrainer, the Expander, the Guide by His obedience, in the trial of people when their desires are qidad (divided)."

Qidad is the plural of qiddah, from qadda, meaning "to cut," as though each path is cut off from the others by its distinctiveness.

﴿And we thought﴾, that is, we now know, ﴿that we would never cause Allah to fail﴾, that is, the matter is that we will never cause Allah, exalted is He, to fail ﴿while we are in the earth﴾, that is, wherever we are in its regions, ﴿nor would we escape Him by fleeing﴾, that is, fleeing from it to the sky. The earth is thus taken in its entirety. Since the phrase "nor would we ..." etc. corresponds to what precedes it, it follows that the flight must be to the sky. In this there is (tarraqqi, ascent or progression) and exaggeration, as if it were said: "We will never cause Him, glorified is He, to fail on earth or in the sky."

It is also permissible that no attention be paid to generality or specificity, as in the phrase "arsalaha al-'irak" (he released her at full gallop), and the failing be taken as two categories, drawn from the word "flight," with the meaning: "We will never cause Him, glorified is He, to fail on earth if He intends a matter concerning us, and we will never cause Him, Mighty and Majestic, to fail by fleeing if we seek [to escape]." The sum of this is that if we seek Him, we do not escape Him, and if we flee, we do not get free of Him, glorified is He. The benefit of mentioning the earth is to depict that, despite its expanse and breadth, there is no refuge from Him, exalted is He, and no place of escape, because of the intensity of His power, glorified is He, and the increase of His authority, exalted is He. Similar to this is the saying of the poet:

"Indeed you are like the night, which will overtake me, even if you think the far place from you is wide."

It has also been said that the benefit of mentioning "the earth" is to depict their settling upon it and the extreme distance of it from the place of His establishment, glorified and exalted is He, but this is not the case.

That "fi al-ard" (in the earth) and "haraban" (by fleeing) are two circumstantial accusatives (hal), as we have indicated, is what the majority of scholars (jumhur) hold. It is also permitted for "haraban" to be a specifying accusative (tamyiz) transferred from the subject, meaning: "Our flight will never cause Him, glorified is He, to fail."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 13:

﴿And indeed, when we heard the guidance﴾, that is, the Qur'an, which is guidance itself, ﴿we believed in it﴾ without hesitation or wavering. ﴿So whoever believes in his Lord﴾ and in what He, mighty and majestic, has sent down, ﴿then he will not fear﴾. The "then" (fa') is the response of the conditional, and the like of it, the negated clause introduced by "lā", may take the fa' or omit it, as stated by him in the commentary on al-Tashil (Sharh al-Tashil). However, omitting it is better, and for this reason a subject (mubtada') is assumed here, so that the sentence is nominal. The fa' becomes obligatory when it is a response, except in what is anomalous, such as the line:

"Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them" (known).

Some (scholars) made the assumption obligatory, believing that the fa' cannot enter into such a construction, meaning: "so he does not fear". ﴿Bakhsan﴾, that is, a diminution in the reward. Al-Raghib said: bakhs is the diminishing of a thing in the manner of injustice. ﴿Nor rahaqan﴾, that is, the overtaking of humiliation, from His saying, exalted is He, (﴿and humiliation will overtake them﴾) [Yunus: 27]. Its root meaning is general overtaking. Al-Raghib said: "rahaqahu al-amr" means it overtook him by force. In al-Asas: "rahaqahu" means it approached him, and "sabiyyun murahiq" means a boy close to puberty. In al-Nihayah it is said: "a man who has rahaq" is one who is quick toward evil and is overtaken by it.

The summary of the meaning is: he does not fear that his right will be diminished, nor that humiliation will overtake him. So the verbal noun, namely ﴿bakhsan﴾, is understood with respect to the object. The meaning is not that the non-believer's right is diminished; rather, the emphasis is on confirming what is due to the believer of reward and its full, complete provision. As for others, they have no share at all, let alone completeness. In this there is the point that what the non-believer is recompensed with is itself diminished, and in relation to this right there is complete diminution, even if there is no diminished right there. Thus in al-Kashf. Or (the verse means): ﴿he does not fear diminution or humiliation﴾, because he has not diminished anyone's right nor overtaken anyone with injustice, so he does not fear the recompense for either. This is not an ellipsis of a noun ("recompense"), rather that is an explanation of the sum of the meaning, and that what is mentioned is in itself frightening, for one may say "I feared the sin and I feared its punishment," because what generates the feared thing is itself feared.

In this there is an indication that the believer, by avoiding diminution and overtaking, does not fear them, for the absence of fear of the feared thing is only due to the absence of the feared thing. It is also possible to interpret it as an ellipsis, and the original sentence would be: "Whoever does not diminish anyone nor overtakes anyone with his injustice, does not fear their recompense." So the sublime wording was put in its place, alerting through the cause to the effect. The first (interpretation), as has been said, is more apparent and closer in its derivation.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding the verse: "He does not fear a reduction of his good deeds nor an increase in his evil deeds."

'Abd ibn Humayd transmitted from Qatadah that he said: "﴿Then he does not fear bakhsan﴾, injustice, by his doing injustice to his good deeds, so that something of them is reduced, ﴿nor rahaqan﴾, nor that the sin of another be laid upon him." A similar report was transmitted from al-Hasan.

Perhaps the first meaning is more fitting to the encouragement to faith, and also to the word rahaq, in view of what you have heard of His saying, ﴿and humiliation will overtake them﴾. Ibn Thabit and al-A'mash recited "fa-la yakhaf" with a jussive, considering "lā" as a prohibition, not a negation, because the response accompanied by the fa' cannot be jussive. It has been said that the fa' is superfluous and "lā" is for negation, but this is nothing. Whatever the case, the first reading is more indicative of the certainty that the believer is surely saved, and that he is the one specifically so, to the exclusion of others. This is because the pronoun "huwa" is set before the verb (as in "huwa 'urf"), and both exclusivity and emphasis are combined in it when the context requires both. Ibn Thabit recited "bakhsan" with a fatha on the kha'.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 14:

﴿And among us are the Muslims, and among us are the qāsiṭūn (those who deviate) from the path of truth, which is faith and obedience.﴾ It is said: "qasata al-rajul" means the man deviated (jāra) when he transgressed, and they recited (poetry):

"A people who killed the son of Hind by force, ʿUmar, and who transgressed (qasaṭū) against al-Nuʿmān."

﴿Then whoever embraces Islam, those are﴾ the demonstrative refers to those who embraced Islam, and the plural is according to the sense. ﴿They sought out﴾ (tahharraw): they aimed for and intended. ﴿A right course﴾ (rashadan): a great one, which brought them to the abode of reward. Al-Aʿraj recited "rushdan" with a damma on the rāʾ and sukūn on the shīn.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 15:

﴿And as for the deviators (al-qasitun), those who turn away from the ways of Islam, they shall be fuel for Hell﴾

They will be kindled with them, just as the disbelieving humans are kindled with them. He (al-Alusi) inclined to the view that ﴿Whoever submits﴾ and what follows is from the speech of the jinn. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "The more likely view is that it is an address from Allah the Exalted to His Prophet (ﷺ), and what comes after the verses supports this."

In al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari), it is said: "Whoever does not hold that the jinn receive reward claims that Allah the Exalted threatened their deviators but did not promise reward to their submitting ones. Yet it is sufficient as a promise that He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Those have sought out the right path﴾, thus mentioning the cause of reward. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is too just to punish the deviator and not reward the rightly guided. This clearly indicates that it is from His own speech, Mighty and Majestic."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And that if they had remained upright on the way﴾ and so on, is certainly coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying, ﴿that he, the listener...﴾ [a reference to the preceding verse, "that it was a party of men among mankind..."; the wording here is "أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ", i.e., "that he [a jinn] listened"]. The advancement of the coordinated element over something else does not harm this view, because the sense is clear and there is no ambiguity. ("And that") is a lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy (thaqilah) form, and its noun is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n).

Al-A'mash and Ibn Wathhab read with a damma on the waw of ﴿lawi﴾ [i.e., "lawu"]. The meaning: "and it was revealed to me that the matter is that if mankind and jinn had remained upright, or both of them, ﴿on the way﴾ which is the religion of Islam, ﴿We would have given them to drink﴾ water ﴿in abundance﴾, that is, plentiful." 'Asim, in the narration of al-A'mash, read with a kasra on the dal [i.e., "ghadiqan" instead of "ghadaqan" in the reading of the word], and the intended meaning is: "We would have widened provision for them." The specific mention of abundant water is because it is the basis of livelihood, and its abundance is the basis of plenty; thus it has been said, "wealth is where water is," and because of the rarity of its availability among the Arabs.

﴿لِنَفْتِنَهم فِيهِ﴾ means: that We may test them, (to see) how they will be thankful for it. That is, We will deal with them in the manner of one who is being tested.

It has also been said: if the jinn had kept to the most excellent way (al-ṭarīqa al-muthlā), that is, if their father, the jinn, had remained upon the worship and obedience of God, the Exalted, and had not been arrogant about prostrating to Adam, and had not disbelieved, and his offspring had followed him in Islam, then ﴿We would surely have given them abundant water﴾ and We would have expanded their provision, so that We might test them. On this view, the pronoun may refer to al-qāsiṭūn (the unjust). This is what is transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and Ibn Jubayr. As for taking the word al-muthlā (in ﴿الطَّرِيقَةِ المُثْلى﴾), it has been said that the definite article is for prior reference (li-l-'ahd), and what is known is the way of the jinn, which is preferred over others. It has also been said that calling it a "way" while considering everything else not a "way" implies that it is preferred.

It has been said that the meaning is: if the jinn kept to their own way, which is disbelief, and did not submit to hearing the Qur'an, then We would have expanded provision for them as a gradual lure (istidrāj), so that We might cast them into trial and punish them for their ingratitude. Something similar is reported from al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Rabī' ibn Anas, Zayd ibn Aslam and Abu Mijlaz, except that they made the pronoun refer to those who had embraced Islam, and said: i.e., if those among the people who had become Muslims were to disbelieve, ﴿We would surely have given them abundant water﴾, and so on. But this contradicts the apparent sense, because "keeping to the way" is used for keeping to disbelief, and the mentioned blessing being a gradual lure without any indicator for it, together with the verse ﴿And if the people of the towns had believed﴾ [al-A'rāf: 96] and so on, supports the first view.

Al-Ṭībī claimed that the closing phrase ﴿عَزَّ وجَلَّ وَمَن يُعْرِضْ عَنْ ذِكْرِ رَبِّهِ﴾ and so on supports what was said, since it is an emphasis on the content of the preceding threat, i.e., "We will lead them gradually so that they follow their desires, which cause insolence and turning away from the remembrance of God, the Exalted." It is open to question. The word dhikr (remembrance) is a verbal noun added to its object, meaning the worship (of God), or it means reminder (tadhkīr) added to its agent, and it is interpreted as admonition. Some have said the intended meaning of dhikr is revelation: that ﴿وَمَن يُعْرِضْ﴾ (whoever turns away) from the worship of his Lord, the Exalted, or from His admonition, Glorified is He, or from His revelation, ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾ (He will make him enter) is taken to imply the meaning of "We cause him to enter," which is why it takes a second object directly, namely His saying ﴿عَذابًا صَعَدًا﴾ (a punishment of ascending torment), without "in" (fī). Or it is of the type of omission and transitivity. Ṣa'ad is a verbal noun described by the word as an intensification or by interpretation, meaning: We will make him enter a punishment that overwhelms the one punished and overpowers him. It was also explained as "hardship": one says "so-and-so is in ṣa'ad concerning his affair," meaning in difficulty. From this is the saying of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him: "Nothing has ever burdened me as much as a marriage proposal burdens me," i.e., it was hard upon me. It seems to be taken from the fact that it was their custom to mention all the qualities of the suitor, inherited and acquired, so it was difficult for him to do so extemporaneously, or it was difficult for him to speak the truth in the face of the suitor and his clan. It has also been said that it was hard because of the faces and the looking of some at others. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn 'Abbas said: "Ṣa'ad is a mountain in Hell." Al-Khudri said: "Whenever they put their hands on it, it melts." 'Ikrimah said: "It is a smooth rock in Hellfire, which they are made to climb; when he reaches its top, he is thrown down into Hell."

On this basis, Abu Ḥayyān said: it is permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for "punishment," with an omitted modifier, i.e., "a punishment that is ṣa'ad (ascending)." It is also permissible for it to be the object of nasluku, and "punishment" to be an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi).

The Kufans read ﴿يَسْلُكْهُ﴾ with yā' (يسلكه), while the rest of the Seven read it with nūn (نسلكه). Ibn Jundub read it with nūn from aslaka. Some of the Successors read it with yā' likewise. These are two dialect forms: salaka and aslaka. A poet describing a defeated army said:

"When they drive them into a narrow place, a scattered throng, as the drovers drive the scattered camels."

Some people read "ṣuʿudan" with two ḍammas. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Ḥasan read it with a ḍamma on the ṣād and a fatḥa on the 'ayn. Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is that there is no rest in it.

And that the mosques belong to Allah ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ لِلَّهِ﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with ﴿أنَّهُ اسْتَمَعَ﴾ ("that he listened"), so it is part of what was revealed. The apparent meaning is that "the mosques" refers to the places prepared for prayer and worship, i.e., "It was revealed to me that the mosques are exclusively for Allah, exalted is His majesty." ﴿فَلا تَدْعُوا﴾ ("so do not invoke") means "so do not worship in them" ﴿مَعَ اللَّهِ أحَدًا﴾ ("alongside Allah anyone"), other than Him, glorified is He.

Al-Hasan said that the intended meaning is every place on the earth where prostration was performed, whether it was prepared for that purpose or not, since the entire earth is a mosque for this community. It seems that this is what is meant by the authentic hadith: "The earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification" (ṭahūr).

It is well known that this is one of the distinctive features of our Prophet (ﷺ), i.e., of his law (sharīʿah), so it belongs to him and to his community (peace and blessings be upon him). Before that, prayer was permitted for them only in churches (biyaʿ) and synagogues (kanāʾis). This was challenged: ʿIsā (peace be upon him) used to travel extensively (yukthiru al-siyāḥah), and other prophets (peace be upon them) journeyed, so if prayer was not permitted to them outside the places mentioned, it would follow that they abandoned prayer at many times, which is far-fetched, especially regarding al-Khiḍr (peace be upon him). For this reason it was said that what is specific is that it is (both) a mosque and a means of purification together (al-majmūʿ), and the specificity of tayammum (dry ablution) suffices for its distinctiveness.

It is answered that the intended specificity is in relation to the earlier nations, not their prophets (peace be upon them). If al-Khiḍr is alive today, then he is from this community, whether he was a prophet or not, based on the report: "If Mūsā were alive, he would have no choice but to follow me." His ruling before becoming a prophet is clear, and the matter concerning him if he was not a prophet is easy.

It was also said that the intended meaning is al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, i.e., the Kaʿbah itself, or the whole sanctuary (al-Ḥaram) according to what has been said. The plural is used because every part of it is a mosque with a specific direction of prayer (qiblah), or because it is the qiblah of mosques: every qiblah faces toward it, so it is treated, metaphorically, as if it were all the mosques.

It was also said that the intended meaning is it and Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). Ibn Abī Ḥātim reported from Ibn ʿAbbās: "On the day ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ لِلَّهِ﴾ etc. was revealed, the earth was not (considered) a mosque, but only al-Masjid al-Ḥarām and the Masjid of Īliyāʾ, Bayt al-Maqdis." The matter of the plural regarding this view is more evident than in the first view, though not that it is like the first, which is contrary to the apparent meaning, and what has been mentioned does not complete as evidence for it.

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jubayr, al-Zajjāj and al-Farrāʾ said that the intended meaning is the seven limbs upon which one prostrates, its singular being masjad (with a fatḥah on the jīm), and they are: the two feet, the two knees, the two palms, and the face, i.e., the forehead and the nose. It is related that al-Muʿtaṣim asked Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī ibn Mūsā al-Kāẓim, may Allah be pleased with them, about this, and he answered with what was mentioned.

It was also said: the prostrations (al-sajadāt), since masjad with a fatḥah on the jīm is a mīmī verbal noun (maṣdar mīmī). It is reported from al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad that His saying, exalted is He, ﴿وأنَّ المَساجِدَ﴾ is with the implicit lām of causation (lām al-taʿlīl), and it is connected to what follows, and "the mosques" carries its well-known meaning, i.e., because ﴿المَساجِدَ لِلَّهِ فَلا تَدْعُوا مَعَ اللَّهِ أحَدًا﴾ ("the mosques are for Allah, so do not invoke alongside Allah anyone"). Since the fāʾ (fa) is not in the answer of a definite condition, it is in reality superfluous (zāʾidah), so there is no prohibition on placing what follows it before it. Indeed, more than one scholar said: it was brought in to imply the meaning of a condition, and the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, loves to be declared one, and not to have anyone associated with Him; so if they do not make Him one in other places, then do not invoke anyone with Him in the mosques, because the mosques are exclusively His, glorified is He, so associating in them is more heinous and even more so. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿لإيلافِ قُرَيْشٍ﴾ ﴿إيلافِهِمْ رِحْلَةَ الشِّتاءِ والصَّيْفِ﴾ ﴿فَلْيَعْبُدُوا﴾ [Quraysh: 1–3], in a certain manner, and this is not counted as a definite condition. The objection that the fāʾ would become meaningless (laghw) is dispelled by what has been mentioned, since it denotes causality, and its meaning is derived from the implicit lām. It was also said in response that it is an emphasis of the lām, or it is superfluous and brought in to indicate its meaning, and that it is implicit.

As for the address in ﴿تَدْعُوا﴾, it was said that it is addressed to the jinn. This is supported by what was narrated from Ibn Jubayr, who said: The jinn said, "O Messenger of Allah, how can we attend the prayer with you when we are far from you?" So the verse was revealed.

[It is addressed] to them, in the sense that your worship, when it is accepted, is only when you do not associate anything in it. It was also said that it is a general address. It is related from Qatādah: "The Jews and Christians, when they entered their churches and synagogues, associated others with Allah, exalted is His majesty, so we were commanded to devote the invocation sincerely to Allah, exalted is He, when we enter the mosques," meaning by this verse.

It is related from Ibn Jurayj, as a substitute ("when we were commanded," etc.): "So He commanded them to declare Him one." What relates to that will also come, if Allah wills. And Ibn Hurmuz and Ṭalḥah read "wa-inna al-masājida" with a kasrah on the hamzah of "inna," and this is taken as a new sentence (istiʾnāf).

[Page 92]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 19:

﴿And that﴾ with the hamza pronounced with a fatha according to the majority, on the basis that it is conjoined with ﴿that he listened﴾, like the one before it, so it is part of His speech, exalted is He; meaning: "and it was revealed to me that the matter..." ﴿when the servant of Allah stood﴾, that is, the Prophet ﷺ. His words, exalted is He, ﴿calling upon Him﴾ are a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to ﴿servant﴾; meaning, when he stood worshipping Him, mighty and majestic is He. That was his standing, upon him be blessings and peace, for the dawn prayer at Nakhla, as has passed.

﴿They were nearly﴾, that is, the jinn, as Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said, ﴿becoming around him a mass (libad)﴾, piling up on top of one another from their crowding around him, out of amazement at what they witnessed of his worship and heard of his recitation, and of his companions following him in standing, bowing and prostrating, because they saw what they had never seen the like of and heard what they had never heard the like of. This appears clearly to indicate that they were many, not nine or thereabouts. As for the mention of him, upon him be blessings and peace, with the word "servant" rather than "Prophet" or "Messenger" or a pronoun, this is either because it is said on his tongue, since he was commanded to say "it has been revealed to me that...", so it was phrased in accordance with what the station of servanthood and humility requires; or because He, exalted is He, deviated from that to draw attention to the fact that worship by a servant is not to be deemed remote. He, upon him be blessings and peace, transmitted His words, glorified is He, as they are, so as to raise himself above any intermediary, for there is no existence for the trace after the essence. Since this deviation on His part, majestic and exalted is He, is either for this or for that, and not a free disposition from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it is not precluded, as some eminent scholars have said: combining the two goods.

Al-Hasan and Qatada said: the pronoun in ﴿they were nearly﴾ refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs. Thus "standing" means standing with the message, and "massing" means massing in enmity. The meaning is: and when the servant of Allah stood with the message, calling to Allah alone and leaving what they used to call upon besides Him, they were nearly, through their mutual support and cooperation in hostility towards him, crowding around him in heaps. It is permitted that the pronoun on this view refers to the jinn and mankind.

Also from Qatada, what it implies: "Mankind and the jinn massed together over this matter to extinguish it, but God, exalted is He, refused except to grant victory to him against whoever opposed him." In al-Bahr, one who says that the servant of Allah here is Noah, peace be upon him, whose people nearly killed him until Allah rescued him from them, is further off the mark, as stated by al-Hasan; and further still is the view of one who says he is Abdullah ibn Salam. By my life, it is not fitting to hold that, and I do not think it has any validity in any respect.

Nafi' and Abu Bakr, as we mentioned, and Ibn Hurmuz and Talha, as in al-Hibr, read ﴿And indeed he﴾ with a kasra on the hamza. It is taken that the clause is a fresh resumptive sentence from His speech, mighty and majestic is He. It is also permitted that it is part of the speech of the jinn, conjoined to the clause ﴿Indeed we heard﴾, in which they related to their people, when they returned to them, what they had seen of the prayer of the Prophet ﷺ and the crowding of his companions around him in following him. This is related from Ibn Jubayr. Something similar is permitted on the reading with fatha, on the basis of what you have heard from Abu Hatim, or with the supposition "and we inform you that he..." or the like.

In al-Kashf: the view, on the supposition that ﴿And that the mosques﴾ is part of what was revealed, that ﴿so do not call upon﴾ is an address to the jinn, reported in speech, if His words, exalted is He, "And indeed when he stood" in the kasra reading are taken as part of the speech of the jinn, lest the composition be broken if it were made the start of a separate story and a separate revelation disconnected from the report of the jinn. Likewise, if the pronoun in ﴿they were nearly﴾ is taken to refer to the jinn in the fatha reading too. The original sense is: "The mosques are for Allah, so do not call upon anyone along with Allah, O jinn." Then it was said: "Say, O Muhammad, to the polytheists of Mecca: ﴿It has been revealed to me﴾ that..." And if this is so, then within the reported speech there comes the affirmation of this ruling with respect to the addressees as well, because the reason is the same. But if it is taken as a general address, the better view is that the pronoun in ﴿they were nearly﴾ refers to the polytheists, or to the jinn and mankind, and that on the kasra reading it is a resumptive sentence, the beginning of a narrative from Him, majestic is His glory, in reporting the condition of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. It serves as a preparation for what follows and a confirmation of what was mentioned before. It is as if it were said: "Say to the polytheists of Mecca what has occurred concerning the jinn, and that some of them believed and others of them disbelieved, so that the relating of this may be a kindness to them in desisting from what they were engaged in, and an incitement to faith." Then it was said: ﴿And indeed when the servant of Allah stood calling upon Him﴾ and declaring Him one, ﴿the two groups of disbelieving jinn and mankind were nearly﴾ ﴿becoming around him a mass﴾, indicating their failure to be restrained despite these clear proofs and luminous signs.

How excellent is the contrast between His words, exalted is He, ﴿And that the mosques﴾ and this statement: as if they were all forbidden from associating partners and called to monotheism, and they responded by hostility towards the one who affirms Allah, glorified is He, and calls upon Him, and were not content with refusing Him alone. This is among the distinctive features of the Noble Book and its wondrous style: when it takes up one story after another, it makes the two equal partners in what the discourse is directed towards, and adds to that the mutual kinship between them.

On the harmony between the end of the first and the opening of the second; and perhaps this aspect has considerable merit. As for interpreting it in accordance with what is reported from al-Khalil, and ﴿And that the mosques are for Allah, so do not call upon...﴾ etc., then the better view is that it is a digression, mentioned after the threat against those who turn away. Taking it to mean the seven limbs is more evident, because in it there is a reminder that He, exalted is He, bestowed them as a favour upon them, and an alert that the wisdom in creating them is the service of the Worshipped One. This is from the point of view of departing from the wording of "limbs" and their specific names to "mosques," and a sign that this contradicts associating partners. In that case, no difficulty remains regarding the connection of what follows with what precedes, on both readings. And the more correct view, and Allah knows best. End of quotation. So reflect.

The word libad, with kasra on the lam and fatha on the ba', as the majority read, is the plural of libda, with kasra, like kisra and kisar, and it means groups. It is likened to a thing whose parts are compacted one upon another. It is also said of locusts, and from it, as al-Jubba'i said, is the verse of 'Abd Manaf ibn Rub' al-Hudhali:

They gathered in six or four hundred, until it was as if upon them was a swarm of locusts, massed.

Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin and Ibn 'Amir, in one report from him, read ﴿lubadan﴾ with a damma on the lam, the plural of lubda, like zubra and zubar. Also from Ibn Muhaysin: sukun on the ba' and damma on the lam. Al-Hasan, al-Jahdari, Abu Haywa and a group from Abu 'Amr read with two dammas, the plural of lubud, like kuhn and ruhn, or the plural of lubud, like subur and sabr. Al-Hasan and al-Jahdari also read, in one report from them, ﴿lubbadan﴾ with a damma on the lam and shaddah on the ba', the plural of labid; and Abu Raja' read with a kasra and a shaddah on the open ba'.

﴿Say: "I only call upon﴾ (aʿbudu, "I worship") ﴿my Lord, and I associate none with Him﴾ in worship ﴿with anyone.﴾ So that is no novelty nor an unusual matter that would call for astonishment or for unanimous hostility toward me. Most readers recited «qāla» (he said), taking it as a quotation from Him, exalted is He, of His Messenger's words (ﷺ) to those who massed against him, or as a quotation from the jinn to him when they returned to their people. So pay attention. The reading of the imperative (quul, "Say") is that of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and Abū ʿAmr according to one of the transmissions from him, and it is more apparent and better suited to His words, glorified is He: ﴿Say: "I have no power to bring you harm or right guidance."﴾ That is, nor benefit. The expression names the cause to mean the effect. The meaning is: I am unable to harm you or to benefit you; the one who harms and the one who benefits is only God, mighty and majestic. Or: I have no power over you, (misguidance (ghayyan) and right guidance (rashadan)). On the reading that "harm" (ḍurran) here means misguidance (ghayy), this is an expression naming the cause for the effect, and it is supported by the reading of Ubayy: «ghayyan» in place of «ḍurran». The meaning is: I am unable to compel you to error or to right guidance; the only one capable of that is God, glorified and exalted. It is also permitted that the verse contains *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which one of two parallel terms is omitted from each side, the other being understood from its counterpart). The original would be: "I have no power over you to harm you or benefit you, nor to lead you astray or guide you," so from each of the two opposites is dropped what is mentioned in the other. And al-Aʿraj read «rushudan» with two dammas.

﴿Say: "I only call upon﴾ (aʿbudu, "I worship") ﴿my Lord, and I associate none with Him﴾ in worship ﴿with anyone.﴾ So that is no novelty nor an unusual matter that would call for astonishment or for unanimous hostility toward me. Most readers recited «qāla» (he said), taking it as a quotation from Him, exalted is He, of His Messenger's words (ﷺ) to those who massed against him, or as a quotation from the jinn to him when they returned to their people. So pay attention. The reading of the imperative (quul, "Say") is that of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, and Abū ʿAmr according to one of the transmissions from him, and it is more apparent and better suited to His words, glorified is He: ﴿Say: "I have no power to bring you harm or right guidance."﴾ That is, nor benefit.
