Or: I have no power over you, (misguidance (ghayyan) and right guidance (rashadan)). On the reading that "harm" (ḍurran) here means misguidance (ghayy), this is an expression naming the cause for the effect, and it is supported by the reading of Ubayy: «ghayyan» in place of «ḍurran». The meaning is: I am unable to compel you to error or to right guidance; the only one capable of that is God, glorified and exalted. It is also permitted that the verse contains *iḥtibāk* (a rhetorical device in which one of two parallel terms is omitted from each side, the other being understood from its counterpart). The original would be: "I have no power over you to harm you or benefit you, nor to lead you astray or guide you," so from each of the two opposites is dropped what is mentioned in the other. And al-Aʿraj read «rushudan» with two dammas.

﴿Say: Indeed, none can protect me from Allah﴾ if He intends harm for me, ﴿and I will not find any refuge besides Him﴾. That is, no one to turn aside to or deviate toward. Al-Kalbi said it means "an entrance into the earth," and al-Suddi said it means "a shelter." Its origin is "al-mudkhal" (the entrance) from "al-lahd" (the burial niche), and what is meant is a refuge one leans upon. They recited:

Alas for my soul, and my soul will not avail me,
and there is no escape from the decree of Allah.

Al-Raghib (al-Raghib al-Isfahani) permitted that it be a noun of place (ism makan) or a verbal noun (masdar). This, as it is said, is an explanation of his (ﷺ) inability regarding his own affairs, after the explanation of his inability regarding the affairs of others. It is also said that the speech contains an omission, which is: They said, "Leave what you call to, and we will protect you." So it was said to him, ﴿Say: Indeed, none can protect me﴾, and so on. It is also said that it is a reply to a statement which is reported: that the chief of the jinn, when they crowded around him, said, "I will drive them away from you." So he said, ﴿Indeed, none can protect me﴾, and so on. Al-Mawardi mentioned this. Both opinions are of no value. And His, the Exalted's, saying:

﴿Except a message from Allah﴾ is an exception (istithna') from the object of ﴿I do not possess﴾, as the words of Qatadah indicate. What lies between them is an emphatic parenthetical clause affirming the negation of ability. There is therefore no objection based on the length of the intervening material, which would make the connection distant. If the meaning is "I do not possess the ability to harm you or to benefit you," then it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil), as if it were said, "I possess nothing except a message." If the meaning is "I do not possess the ability to compel you to error or to right guidance," then it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), or it is of the type of the line: "And there is no fault in them / except that their swords..."

[p. 94]

...as in al-Kashshaf. The apparent meaning of the words of some eminent scholars is that it is either a connected exception from ﴿right guidance﴾, since conveying the message is guidance and benefit, and an exception from the conjoined item (al-ma'tuf) without the item it is conjoined to (al-ma'tuf 'alayhi) is permissible; or it is a disconnected exception from ﴿a refuge﴾. Al-Razi said: because the message from Allah, Exalted is He, cannot be included under His saying ﴿besides Him, a refuge﴾, for it is not from besides Allah, glory be to Him, but from Him, exalted is He, and by His aid and His enabling.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), al-Hasan said it is a disconnected exception, meaning: ﴿none will protect me﴾ [any] one, but [only] if My mercy reaches me through that. Protection (al-ijarah) is used metaphorically for conveying, since it is the cause of Allah's protection and His mercy, glory be to Him. It was also said that, on this meaning, it is a connected exception.

The meaning is: I will not find anything I can incline toward and take refuge in except that I convey and obey, and then He protects me. Its accusative case may be as an exception from ﴿a refuge﴾, or as a badal (substitute). The latter is the better view, since it is preceded by a negation. Al-Zajjaj parsed it as a substitute. End of quotation. The more apparent is what has preceded.

It was said that illa is compounded of the conditional particle in (أنّ) and the negative la (لا), and the meaning is: "that I do not convey a message," and what precedes it indicates the response. It is like your saying: "except standing, then sitting." Its apparent meaning is that the verbal noun (the masdar) takes the place of the condition, like a governed element (ma'mul) of kana. There is a discussion among the grammarians about omitting the conditional clause while the particle remains, and the apparent view is that the regularity of its omission is conditional on the retention of la, as in his saying:

"So divorce her, for you are not a match for her; and if not, the sword will reach your forehead."

This holds as long as no element takes its place, such as a governed element or an explanatory element, like ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection﴾ [al-Tawbah: 6], and "people will be recompensed for their deeds: if good, then good." This view runs contrary to what is most immediately understood, as is not hidden.

Allah's saying ﴿and His messages﴾ is conjoined to ﴿a message﴾. The phrase ﴿from Allah﴾ is attached to an elided element that functions as an adjective to it, i.e., a message proceeding from Allah. It is not a complement to it, because the word is used with ʿan (عن), as in his saying (ﷺ): «Convey from me, even if it is one verse.»

The meaning, as you know from the earlier discussion of the exception, is: "I do not possess for you anything except conveying, [a conveying] proceeding from Him, Exalted is He, and His messages, with which the Mighty and Majestic has sent me."

In al-Kashshaf: there is an elision in the speech, i.e., the conveying of His message. The original speech was "except the conveying of the messages of Allah," but it was changed to this form to indicate the two conveyings, as an exaggeration. Each of the two meanings, namely that it is from Allah, Exalted is He, and that it is the conveying of His messages, requires diligence in it. End of quotation.

In the wording of al-Kashshaf there is an allusion to what he indicated. But it was objected to: it is not proper to posit the elided noun here, namely "conveying" (balagh), for then the conjunction would be the conjoining of a thing to itself. This could be justified by saying that the conveying from Allah is what He gave him without intermediary, while the conveying of the messages is what is contained in them. But this is extremely far-fetched, so understand.

Abu Hayyan preferred conjoining it to the sacred name. He said: the apparent reading is that ﴿His messages﴾ is conjoined to ﴿Allah﴾, meaning: "except that I convey from Allah and from His messages." Its apparent meaning is that min (مِنْ) is in the sense of ʿan (عَنْ), though it was earlier stated from him that it indicates the starting point (ibtida' al-ghayah).

It was read: "qala: la amliku" (he said: I do not possess), meaning that ʿAbd Allah (the Prophet) said it to the polytheists, or to the jinn. He also allowed that it could be a quotation from the jinn to their people.

As for the connection of this verse with what precedes it: it was said, based on the view that talabbud (تَلَبُّد, massing together) means enmity, that when they massed against him (ﷺ) displaying enmity, it was said to him: ﴿Say: I do not possess for you harm or right guidance﴾. That is, I only wanted your benefit, and you repaid me with hostility. It is not within my power to bring about the benefit I wanted, nor the harm with which I would repay you; rather, both belong to Allah Most High. In this is a great threat and a referral of matters to Allah, Exalted is He, and that He, glory be to Him, is the one who will recompense him for his good conduct and their bad conduct. Furthermore, there is exaggeration in it, in that he does not abandon conveying because of their massing, for what he is able to do is convey, and one does not abandon what is within one's capacity. Therefore He said ﴿except a message﴾. On this view, making it a substitute for ﴿a refuge﴾ is strongly antithetical, and the conditional is close to it. As for if the address is to the jinn and the talabbud is out of wonder, the best view is that when they massed for that reason, it was said to him (ﷺ): "Say to them: What is the matter with you that you crowd around me in wonder at me and at the devotion of my companions to worship? To me belongs neither benefit nor harm; I am only a conveyer from the One who harms and benefits. So turn to worship as we do, and do not turn to wonder. For wonder is at one who turns away from the Bestower, the Avenger, the One who harms and benefits."

Perhaps, considering the strength of the connection, it requires that the massing was more likely due to enmity and disobedience to the Messenger (ﷺ): ﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾, that is, regarding the command to monotheism, since the discussion is about it. Thus the Mu'tazilah and others cannot validly use this verse as evidence for the eternal punishment of sinners in the Fire. He also allowed that "the Messenger" might mean the messenger of the angels, peace be upon them, not the messenger of humankind. Then disobedience to him would mean not conveying to the addressee what reached him in the way it reached him. This is contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿Then indeed for him is the Fire of Hell, abiding therein﴾: that is, in the Fire or in Hell. The plural ﴿abiding﴾ (khalidin) is by consideration of the meaning of ﴿whoever﴾ (man), just as the singular earlier was by consideration of its wording. Had it been considered here too, it would have said khaliden (singular), ﴿forever﴾ (abadan), without end.

Talhah read fa-anna (فَأنَّ) with a fatha on the hamza, on the basis that the reckoning is, as Ibn al-Anbari and others said, "so its recompense is that for him..." etc. The grammarians have explicitly stated that anna (أنَّ) after the conditional fa' (فَ) may be read with fatha or with kasra. Therefore Ibn Mujahid's statement that "no one read it [so]" and that it is a solecism (lahn) arises from his limited tracing of readings and his weakness in grammar.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Until, when they see that which they are promised, then they will know who is weaker in helper and fewer in number﴾ is a conditional clause joined with the initial ḥattā (ḥattā al-ibtidā'iyyah, "until" introducing a new sentence). Although it is not a preposition governing a noun here, it carries the sense of a limit (ghāyah), so what follows it is a limit for something omitted, which is indicated by the state of the disbelievers' weakening of his helpers, peace and blessings be upon him, and their considering his number insignificant. It is as if it were said: they will continue to weaken and mock [the believers] until, when they see what they are promised of the various kinds of punishment in the Hereafter, it becomes clear to them who is the weak one. The apodosis of the conditional also indicates this, and likewise what has been said, "upon what has been said," because His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Say: I only call upon my Lord﴾ is an allusion to the polytheists, however it is estimated. Rather, the noble surah from its beginning is directed toward allusion to the condition of the polytheists of Mecca, as consolation for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and solace for him, peace and blessings be upon him, and as a reproach to them for the shortness of their insight compared with the jinn, despite their claim to acuteness, their lack of fairness, and their confronting [the Prophet] with denial and mockery instead of the jinn's confronting [him] with belief and seeking guidance.

It is permissible to make that a limit for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they would almost become a mass upon him﴾, if it is interpreted as "massing together in enmity." There is no obstacle to the intervention of matters that are not foreign between the limit and that which it limits.

As for Abu Hayyan's saying that it is very remote because of the lengthy separation between them by many sentences, it is worthless, as is his making it a limit for what the preceding sentence contained, meaning: ﴿for him is the fire of Hell﴾, from the wisdom of the fire's being his. Similar to this is what has been said, that it is a limit for something omitted, and the estimate is: "Leave them until, when they see..." etc.

The apparent reading is that (man) is interrogative, as we have indicated, and it is the subject (mubtada'), and (aḍ'afu) is the predicate (khabar), and the clause is in a position of accusative governed by what precedes it, and it has been suspended from operating because of the presence of the interrogative. He also permitted it to be a relative pronoun in a position of accusative governed by (ya'lamūn), with (aḍ'afu) being the predicate of an omitted subject, and the clause being the relative clause (ṣilah) of (man). The estimate is: "they will know him who is the weakest." The omission of the first part of the relative clause is good because of its length, being clarified by the specification (tamyīz). He also permitted interpreting (mā yū'adūn) as the Day of Badr, but the first view is preferred because the apparent is that...

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 25:

His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Say: I do not know﴾, meaning: I do not know, ﴿whether what you are promised is near, or whether my Lord will appoint for it a term (amad)﴾. This is a response to what the polytheists said upon hearing that. The state of affairs implies that they said, in denial and mockery, "When will this promised thing happen?" Rather, it is narrated from Muqatil that al-Nadr ibn al-Harith said that, so it was said: "Say: it will certainly come to pass, but as for its time, I do not know when it will be." The more fitting thing for their question is this answer, intending that which is on the Day of Resurrection, against those who deny it with the utmost denial. Its time is hidden from creation to the utmost degree of concealment. By "amad" is meant a long period of time, by the indication of its contrast with "near". Otherwise, linguistically, it includes both. For this reason it is described as "baeedan" (distant) in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿She wishes that between her and it were a long distance (amadan baeedan)﴾ [Al 'Imran: 30]. It has been said that the meaning of nearness indicates approaching the end, as if it were said: "I do not know whether it is a state expected at every hour, or whether it is deferred, with a limit set for it." The first is preferable and closer.

[Page 96]

﴿عالِمُ الغَيْبِ﴾ (Knower of the unseen) is read in the nominative (*bil-raf'*) as the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject), meaning: He, glory be to Him, is the Knower of the unseen. Abu Hayyan permitted it to be an appositive substitute (*badal*) for ﴿رَبِّي﴾ (my Lord), and others also permitted it to be an explanatory apposition (*bayan*) for it. The fa' in His saying, ﴿فَلا يُظْهِرُ عَلى غَيْبِهِ أحَدًا﴾ (so He does not disclose His unseen to anyone), rules out both of these possibilities, since the structure would then become: ﴿أمْ يَجْعَلُ﴾ (or does He appoint) for Him, the Knower of the unseen, a term, ﴿فَلا يُظْهِرُ عَلى غَيْبِهِ أحَدًا﴾, and this contains a disruption of meaning that is not hidden.

The annexation (*idafah*) of ʿālim (knower) to al-ghayb (the unseen) is a safeguard for the intended sense of constancy in this attribute, so the definiteness of both terms conveys exclusivity (*takhsis*). The definiteness of al-ghayb is for comprehensiveness (*istighraq*). In al-Radi's work it is stated that a generic noun (*ism al-jins*), by which I mean one that applies to the few and the many with a singular form, when used without a contextual indicator (*qarinah*) specifying it to some of what it applies to, is apparently for the comprehensiveness of the genus, based on the inductive study of their speech. Thus the meaning of "the dirt is dry" and "the water is cold" is that everything in which these two realities are found is in such a state. So if you said, regarding their saying "sleep breaks ablution," that sleep while sitting does not break it, you would be contradicting that statement.

This supports the intended meaning here, because the unseen, like water, applies to the few and the many with a single form. Its pluralization as ghuyūb (unseens) does not harm this, just as the pluralization of water as miyāh (waters) does not harm it. Likewise, what is meant by "His unseen" is all of His unseen. ʿIzmī-zādah explicitly stated this, giving as the reason that the annexed generic noun is in the position of a noun with the definite article (*al-*), especially when it originally is a verbal noun (*masdar*). He attributed to the Sharh al-Maqasid what implies this.

It may also be said that this is understood from considering the annexation as referring to a known (*ʿahd*) matter, where the known matter is the comprehensive unseen, or from considering it as expressing exclusivity, where the unseen exclusive to Him is the unseen whose knowledge is exclusive to Him, glory be to Him, which is every unseen. Out of concern for the matter of exclusivity, the explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun. The sentence is a resumptive clause (*istīnāf*) to repel the supposition of a deficiency in the one who denies knowing, and the fa' indicates that the non-disclosure follows from His sole possession of knowledge of the unseen. What is meant by the negated disclosure is complete knowledge through which the reality of the situation is fully unveiled, as the preposition ʿalā (over/upon), which indicates elevation, suggests. It is as if it were said: What is my responsibility if I say, "I do not know whether that appointed unseen time is near or far"? God, glory be to Him and exalted, alone is the Knower of every unseen. So He does not reveal to any of His creatures complete knowledge of that exclusive matter, so that this is more fitting to His exclusivity and further from the supposition that the knowledge of His creatures equals His knowledge, glory be to Him. He, exalted in majesty, reveals only a part of it to whomever He wills, what wisdom requires, which is the axis of all His acts, mighty and majestic. What I have denied knowing of it, of what God has not informed me of, is because revealing it is not something that legislative wisdom requires, the wisdom around which the sphere of the message revolves. Rather, its revelation would undermine that wisdom. If you wish, consider the sentence as occurring in the position of a justification (*ta'lil*) for the earlier denial of knowledge.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 27:

When the flow of the discourse is such that one might suppose from it that he, upon him be blessings and peace, had no knowledge whatsoever of the unseen, the Mighty and Majestic (ʿazza wa jall) followed the speech with an exceptive clause of disconnection (al-istithna' al-munqati', the exception not belonging to the same category as what precedes), as is narrated in al-Bahr from Ibn ʿAbbas, which has the meaning of istidrak (a corrective "but" that introduces a qualification).

This removes that supposition in the most eloquent manner, since He generalized the matter to the chosen messengers, and placed the manner of disclosure in the position of disclosure, while indicating a part of what they were informed of, one suited to the station of the call. So the Mighty, the Speaker said: ﴿Except for whomever He has approved of among messengers; for indeed, He sends before him and behind him guards﴾. That is: but the approved messenger, the Majestic and Exalted One discloses to him some of the unseen matters connected to his mission, as the statement "whomever He has approved of among messengers" indicates a connection of some kind to the messenger. This is either because it is among the foundations of the mission, such as being a miracle (mu'jizah), or because it is among its pillars and rulings, such as the general legal obligations (al-taklifat al-shar'iyyah), the modes of actions, their recompenses, and similar unseen matters whose explanation is among the functions of the mission. He makes guards from the angels, peace be upon them, march in every direction before and behind him, protecting him from the interference of the devils with what He wishes him to be informed of, whether by snatching (ikhtitaf) or by confusing (takhlit).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 28 (part 1 of 2):

﴿That he may know﴾ is connected to ﴿He makes to proceed﴾ and is its purpose. The pronoun refers to "whom": that is, in order that the chosen Messenger may know that ﴿they have indeed conveyed﴾, that is, that the matter has indeed been conveyed to him by the guardians, and that he may believe this with a firm, established belief that corresponds to reality. ﴿That they have indeed conveyed﴾: the matter is that the guardians have indeed conveyed ﴿the messages of their Lord﴾. This is of the type of the saying "The Banu Tamim killed Zayd" (بَنُو تَمِيمٍ قَتَلُوا زَيْدًا), since in reality there is one conveyor with them, namely Jibril (peace be upon him), as is well known, that he is the conveyor among the angels (peace be upon them) to the prophets. ﴿The messages of their Lord﴾ are the unseen matters that are revealed to them as they are, without snatching or confusion. On this view, the "who" (مَن) is a subject, and the clause ﴿Indeed He makes to proceed﴾ is its predicate. The fa' (فَ) was used because it is a relative pronoun.

And His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿and He encompasses what is with them﴾, that is, what is with the guardians, ﴿and has counted everything in number﴾, that is, of what has been and of what will be, ﴿in number﴾, that is, one by one. It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of ﴿He makes to proceed﴾, with or without the particle qad (قَدْ). It was brought for greater emphasis on the matter of His knowledge of all things, and His singularity, glorified is He, in that, in the most complete manner, such that the angels, who are the intermediaries of knowledge, do not share with Him, glorified is He, in that. It is as if it were said: "But the chosen Messenger is made to know by Allah, exalted is He, through the angels, some of the unseen matters that have some connection to his mission, while the fact is that He, exalted is He, has encompassed in knowledge all the circumstances of those intermediaries." And He, may He be exalted and majestic, knows all things in a particular, detailed way; so where are the intermediaries in comparison with Him, exalted is He?

Or it is a circumstantial clause from the subject of ﴿they have conveyed﴾; it was brought to indicate that the guardians themselves did not add or subtract in what they conveyed. It is as if it were said: "So that the Messenger may know that the guardians have conveyed to him the messages of his Lord, while Allah, exalted is He, has known all their circumstances and has known everything. So if they had added or subtracted at the time of conveying, He, glorified is He, would know it, and so He would not choose them for the guarding and watching." This is what came to my limited mind in interpreting these noble verses, and I am not certain of its matter. However, the use of His saying, glorified is He, ﴿so He does not reveal﴾, etc., as evidence for denying the karamat (miraculous favors bestowed upon saints) through being informed of some unseen matters, is not complete, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He does not reveal His unseen to anyone﴾ is in the sense of a particular negative proposition, since a term that conveys generality has entered into the scope of negation. Its most common usage is for negating generality, and this was stated in relation to it in Sharh al-Maqasid (the commentary on al-Maqasid), not for the generality of negation; and that is a particular negation. It therefore does not contradict a particular affirmation, such as that some of the unseen might be revealed to a saint, as some of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni scholars) said concerning His saying, exalted is He, ﴿vision does not perceive Him﴾ [al-An'am: 103].

And it should not be objected that the exception requires that the chosen Messenger be made to know all of His, exalted is He, unseen, on the basis that negation followed by exception implies the affirmation of the opposite of the excluded part, and the opposite of a particular negative is a universal affirmative. This is with the fact that He, glorified is He, does not reveal any person, whoever he may be, to all that He, glorified and exalted is He, knows of the unseen. This is because the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭi'), as Ibn 'Abbas explicitly stated. Likewise, it should not be objected that Allah, exalted is He, negated the revelation of any part of His unseen to anyone except the Messenger, so it follows that He, glorified is He, does not reveal any of it to any of the angels. This is because "the Messenger" here refers specifically to the human Messenger, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for indeed He makes to proceed﴾, etc., and that is only in him, as will not be hidden from one who knows the wisdom of this. And it would follow that He does not reveal any of it to any of the prophets who are not messengers, on the basis of taking the specific meaning of "Messenger" here; and this is for what we mentioned first. Likewise, it should not be objected that it follows that the chosen Messenger is not made to know any of the unseen matters that are not connected to his mission, and that revealing them does not contradict legislative wisdom. This is because there is no restriction of the revealed part to what is connected with the mission, and only the connected part was pointed out because the context required it. Whether every unseen matter revealed to the Messenger must be connected to his mission is a matter open to question.

For the exegetes here there is a discussion that is not objectionable to mention, with what can be said for it and against it, as far as possible. Then the matter after that is up to you. We say: since the view of most Ahl al-Sunnah is the affirmation of the karamat of the saint through being informed of the unseen, and since the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Knower of the unseen, so He does not reveal﴾, etc., indicates its negation, for this reason al-Zamakhshari said: "In this is the refutation of karamat," meaning in general, namely that which consists of revelation of the unseen. This is because those to whom it is attributed, even if they are saints who are approved, are not messengers. And Allah, exalted is He, has singled out the messengers among the approved ones for being informed of the unseen, and for the refutation of soothsaying and astrology, because their practitioners are the furthest thing from approval and the most deserving of wrath. End of quotation.

The Mu'tazili's proof for his doctrine was refuted (lit. they helped and accused and affirmed and cursed) in interpreting the verse in a way that does not contradict their doctrine and that his argument from it is not complete. Al-Imam (Fakhr al-Din al-Razi) said: "There is no general formula in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿concerning His unseen﴾, so it suffices in acting upon its requirement that Allah, exalted is He, not reveal to His creation any single one of His unseen matters. We therefore interpret it as referring to the time of the occurrence of the Resurrection, so the meaning of the verse is that He, exalted is He, does not reveal this unseen matter to anyone, and there remains in the verse no indication that He, glorified is He, does not reveal any of the unseen matters to anyone. This is confirmed by the verse coming after His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Say: I do not know whether what you are promised is near﴾, and what is meant by it is the occurrence of the Day of Resurrection." Then he said: "If it is said: when you interpret that as referring to the Resurrection, how then does He, glorified is He, say ﴿except a messenger whom He has approved﴾, when He does not reveal this unseen matter to any of His messengers? We say: rather, He reveals it near the establishment of the Resurrection. And how could it not be, when He, exalted is He, has said ﴿and the day the sky is split open with clouds and the angels are sent down in descent﴾ [al-Furqan: 25]; and there is no doubt that the angels know at that time." Also, it is possible that this exception is disjunctive, as if it were said: ﴿Knower of the unseen, so He does not reveal concerning His unseen﴾, the specific one, which is the establishment of the Resurrection, ﴿to anyone﴾. Then it was said: ﴿except a messenger whom He has approved, for indeed He makes to proceed before him and behind him﴾ guardians who guard him from the evil of the rebellious jinn and humans. End of quotation.

It has been objected that the word "concerning His unseen" (فِي غَيْبِهِ) contains a term indicating generality, as you heard at the beginning, and the context does not prevent it, unless one contests this. Also, the apparent meaning of his first answer to the objection is that what is meant by "the Messenger" in the verse is the angelic Messenger, and what follows, namely His saying, exalted is He, ﴿for indeed He makes to proceed﴾, etc., rejects this. Moreover, the knowledge of the angels of the time of the Hour on the day the sky splits is not part of revelation concerning the unseen; rather it is part of the bringing out of the unseen and its manifestation to the witnessed, like the revelation of rain at its descent, and what is in the wombs at its birth, and so on. Also, the disjunction in the manner that he mentioned is very far-fetched, since it entirely severs the connection between what precedes and what follows. Unless it is said that such a thing does no harm in a disjunctive exception.

It has also been said that the revelation of the unseen means being informed of it in the most complete manner, such that it yields the highest degrees of knowledge. What is meant is the generality of negation, and it does no harm in this that a term indicating generality has entered the scope of negation, because the rule is that it is usually so, not invariably, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾ [al-Hadid: 23], and His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Allah does not love every disbelieving sinner﴾ [al-Baqarah: 276].

Al-Allamah al-Taftazani explicitly stated this. So the meaning is: ﴿so He does not reveal concerning﴾ any of ﴿His unseen to anyone﴾, ﴿except a messenger whom He has approved﴾, for indeed He, glorified is He, reveals to him some of His unseen, by making to proceed, etc. The karamat of the saint are not an objection, since they are not part of the revelation mentioned, because the saint does not attain the highest degree of knowledge of the unseen that he reports; rather he attains only truthful suppositions or something similar. Likewise is the case with others of the practitioners of spiritual exercises among the disbelievers and others.

It has been objected that among the Sufis there are those who said, such as Shaykh Muhyi al-Din (may God sanctify his secret), that an angel descends upon the saint and informs him of some unseen matters at times; and what points to his descent upon him is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed those who say: "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast﴾ [Fussilat: 30; al-Ahqaf: 13], etc. And that what the saint then attains is a supposition or something like it, and not knowledge like the knowledge attained by the Messenger through the angel, is not free from dispute. Indeed, it may be attained by him through inspiration (ilham) and a breath cast into the heart, similar to what is attained by the Messenger. Also, it would follow that the angel is not revealed concerning the unseen, since the excepted Messenger is the messenger of humans according to the apparent meaning. And to maintain that he is not revealed in the sense previously mentioned, while he is revealed through the intermediary of the angel, is something without any basis at all. Also, it would follow that what is attained by a prophet who is not a messenger, in the narrower sense which is what is understood here, is not knowledge in the sense mentioned; and this, as you see, is unacceptable.

It has been said that what is meant by "the unseen" in both places is the genus, and the revelation concerning it is as you have heard; and likewise the non-occurrence of karamat and the discussion about it are like the discussion of what preceded, with additions. The author of al-Kashf said, in refuting al-Zamakhshari: "The unseen, if it is defined by what he defined it as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿who believe in the unseen﴾ [al-Baqarah: 3], then the verse is a proof against him, because he permitted there that it may be known through Allah's informing or through His establishing of an indicator." And this second part, namely the rational kind, is negated by the verse, and it indicates that the refinement of the methods of proofs is also through the intermediary of the prophets (peace be upon them), and that reason is not independent. The Ahl al-Sunnah, all of them, agree that the unseen in that sense is not known except by a messenger or one who takes from them. And there is nothing in this that negates karamat at all. If what is meant is the absent from the senses in the present moment, without qualification, then restriction is necessary by consensus, so there is nothing in it that negates them either. And if it is defined as the nonexistent, as he mentioned in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ [al-An'am: 73] and elsewhere, then restriction is also necessary. Likewise, if it is defined as what is absent from the servants, or as the hidden. Moreover, the apparent meaning of the verse is that He, exalted is He, is the Knower of every unseen alone, and does not reveal to anyone His unseen that is specific to Him; and that is related to His essence and attributes, exalted and majestic is He, by the indication of the idafah (genitive construction), except to a messenger. And this is so, for His unseen, exalted is He, is not made known except by informing from a messenger, whether angelic or human. Yet not all of His specific unseen is made known; rather only part of it, and a very small part of it. So the implication indicates that other than this specific kind of unseen, there is no prohibition on Allah's making a non-messenger aware of it. This is the apparent meaning of the verse without strained interpretation.

Then, even if it is granted, the second [interpretation] is either comprehensive, and if He, glorified is He, says that He does not reveal all of it to anyone except a chosen messenger, it does not indicate that it is impermissible for a non-messenger to be informed of part of it; or it is unrestricted, and it applies to its perfect form, and so it returns to what we have chosen. The indication of the honour of the idafah and the indication of generality support each other, so there is no justification for hanging it on this verse. And from this it becomes clear that the argument from the verse against the refutation of soothsaying and astrology is not valid, even though their refutation is true. Indeed, one who denies it would be far from the mark, let alone one who declares disbelief in whoever says that it indicates life or death, because he has disbelieved in this verse, as our shaykh al-Tibi transmitted from al-Wahidi,
[p. 99]
al-Zajjaj, and the author of al-Mutli'. End of quotation.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 72, verse 28 (part 2 of 2):

He examined it, arguing that interpreting "his unseen" (ghaybihi) as the unseen specific to Him, meaning what pertains to His essence and attributes, Mighty and Majestic is He, is something that does not suit the context. And [he argued] that the apparent meaning of what he established on the possibility of the all-encompassing (istighraq) interpretation requires, on the assumption that the exception is connected (ittisal al-istithna'), and the affirmation of the opposite of what was negated for the exception, that the Messenger would become aware of all of the unseen of the Most High, up to what becomes apparent through reflection.

The Allamah al-Baydawi first mentioned what is understood from it, according to what has been said: interpreting "his unseen" as general with specificity, i.e., the general unseen that is exclusively His, Most High, knowledge. He interpreted "so He does not reveal" as negating generality, and interpreting "the Messenger" as the human messenger, and considering the exception as disconnected (munqati'), on the basis that the meaning is: ﴿so He does not reveal﴾ to anyone ﴿His unseen﴾ that is exclusive to His, Most High, knowledge ﴿to anyone﴾ ﴿except whom He has chosen of a messenger﴾, so He reveals to him some of His unseen, so that his informing of it is a miracle; thus the argument from the verse to deny the karamah (saintly wonder) is not complete.

The exclusivity has been explained as: He knows it by Himself, but with true, certain knowledge, without a cause, unlike the knowledge of others, for none knows it except Him, glorified is He. As for the knowledge of others of some of it, it is not knowledge of the unseen except in an apparent sense, and with respect to some humans.

It has also been said that by the unseen exclusive to Him, Most High, is meant what no evidence has been set up for, and the knowledge of another of it through His, Most High, informing him does not detract from the exclusivity, since it is relative with respect to one who does not know.

He said secondly, in the answer to the argument, and perhaps he meant the answer according to the people, the following text: "Its answer is the restriction of the Messenger to possession and revelation through what occurs without intermediary, and the karamat of the saints concerning the unseen occur only by receiving from the angels, i.e., by the inspiration into the heart (nafth fi al-ruw') and the like."

Its summary is that the argument is complete only if it is established that the intended meaning of "Messenger" is the messenger of humans and angels together, or the messenger of humans only, and that "revelation" means revelation through an intermediary or not; and all of this is disputed, for it is possible that the Messenger is restricted to the messenger of angels, and that by revelation is meant revelation without intermediary, and the meaning would be: He does not reveal without intermediary of His unseen except to the messengers of the angels; and this does not negate the revelation of the saints of His unseen, because it occurs only through an intermediary. This is an answer by denying both premises, although it would suffice to deny one of them, as al-Imam (al-Razi) and al-Taftazani did in their commentary on al-Maqasid. It has been criticized: human messengers may also be informed without intermediary, and the story of the Mi'raj and the speaking of Musa (peace be upon him) suffice for that. Furthermore, it has been said against this after what was said. And the strangest thing said in this context is that "illa" in His, Most High, saying ﴿except whom He has chosen﴾ is for coordination (lil-'atf).

The meaning is: none reveals His unseen, nor whom He has chosen of a messenger, and his condition is not hidden. Then, the interpretation of His, Most High, saying ﴿for indeed He sends forth﴾ etc. in the manner you have heard is what most of the exegetes adhere to, and the guardians who descend with Jibril, peace be upon him, upon our Prophet ﷺ were four, according to what Ibn al-Mundhir and a group related from Ibn Jubayr. Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn Abbas, who said: Allah, Most High, did not send down to His Prophet ﷺ a verse of the Qur'an except that with it were four angels guarding it until they delivered it to the Prophet ﷺ; then he recited ﴿Knower of the unseen﴾ the verse.

With revelation there may be more than that. In some reports it is said that with Surat al-An'am descended seventy thousand angels, and what has come concerning the verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi) has come. Ibn Kamal said: a subtle point occurred to my dull mind, of the kind rarely found in the pages of books, and it is that what is meant by ﴿before him﴾ in the verse is the outward faculties, and ﴿behind him﴾ the inward faculties; and for this reason He, glorified is He, said ﴿He sends forth﴾ etc., i.e., guardians of the angels enter who guard his outward and inward faculties from the devils, and protect him from their whisperings from those two directions. And if what was meant were guardians from the sides, so that the devils would not approach him at the descent of revelation, and [thus] receive other than the revelation, or hear it and convey it to the soothsayers, who would inform of it before the Messenger's informing, as the author of al-Taysir and others held, the composition of the speech would not be in the manner mentioned, for the expression ﴿He sends forth﴾ etc. ... And the specification of the two mentioned directions only suits what we have mentioned, not what they mentioned. End quote. It is not hidden that this is a kind of allusion. Perhaps the expression "sends forth" (yasluku), according to the interpretation of the majority, is to depict the directions from which the devils come, through narrow gaps and fine passages; and in that there is what beauty there is.

Many have gone to the view that the pronoun in ﴿li-ya'lama﴾ refers to God, Most High, and the pronoun in ﴿abla'u﴾

either refers to the watchers or to "man artada," and the plural is by consideration of the meaning of "man," just as the singular in the two pronouns before it is by consideration of its wording. The meaning is that He, Most High, sends them forth in order that He may know that the matter is that they have conveyed the messages of their Lord, a knowledge entailing recompense, which is that He, Most High, knows it as existing and actualized, as in His, Most High, saying ﴿until We know the strivers﴾ [Muhammad: 31]. So the ultimate purpose is in reality the conveying and the striving, and the mention of His knowledge is to display His, Most High, concern with these two matters, to indicate the recompense that follows from them, to exaggerate in urging them, and to warn against negligence in them. His, Most High, saying ﴿and He has encompassed﴾ etc. is either a coordination with "so He does not reveal," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yasluku," brought to repel the suspicion and to confirm His, Most High, independence in knowledge through the conveying from what was mentioned of the sending forth of the watchers in the manner stated; or it is a coordination, as some claimed, on an implied element, because "li-ya'lama" includes the meaning of "'alima," so the meaning becomes "He has known that and encompassed," etc. It was also permitted that the pronoun of "ya'lama" refers to the Messenger to whom revelation is made, and the pronoun of "abla'u" to the watchers descending to him with revelation.

It is related from Ibn Jubayr what supports this; or [the pronoun refers] to other messengers. "And He has encompassed" etc. is a coordination with "abla'u" or with "la yuzhiru." And from Mujahid: "that He may know whoever denied and associated [partners]" that the messengers had conveyed; and there is in this from remoteness what there is. And according to this, this knowledge does not occur regarding what is in the sea except in the Hereafter. It was said: "that Iblis may know that the messengers have conveyed"; and it was said: "that the jinn may know that the messengers have conveyed what was sent down to them, and they were not the ones receiving it by eavesdropping." Both sayings, as you see, [are weak]. The accusative of "'adadan" according to a group is a specifier (tamyiz) transferred from the object; the original was "ahsa 'adada kulli shay'," except that Abu Hayyan said there is a dispute regarding whether it is established in the language of the Arabs. You know that the transfer in such a case is notional. It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial clause, i.e., counted and restricted, and the indefiniteness of its referent does not harm, since it is for generality; and that it be in the accusative as a verbal noun in the sense of "ihsa'" (counting). So reflect on all of that, and Allah, Most High, is the one who grants success to following the best of paths.

It is read "'alimu" in the nominative (raf') with the accusative for praise, and "'alima" as a past verb with "al-ghayba" in the accusative. Ibn Abbas and Zayd ibn Ali read "li-yu'lama" in the passive voice; al-Zuhri and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "li-yu'lima" with a damma on the ya' and a kasra on the lam, from the causative (i'lam), i.e., that Allah, Most High, may inform whom He wills to inform that they have conveyed, etc. Abu Haywa read "risalata" in the singular. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "uhita" and "uhsiya," each in the passive voice in both verbs, and the raising of "kulla" by substitution (niyaba), while the agent is Allah, Glorified and Mighty is He; so He, glorified is He, is the one who encompasses all circumstances in knowledge and the one who counts everything in number.
